records.title: Aging Service Organizational Capacity to Deliver Evidence-Based Depression Programs: A National Survey
records.abstract: Integration of mental health programs within community-based, social or aging service organizations has been recommended to serve more older adults with depression.  The purpose of this study was to obtain input from aging service organizations across the United States regarding their consideration and resource needs for implementing a lay-led program for depression ( “Do More, Feel Better,” DMFB).  An online survey distributed via email inquired about perceived need and consideration regarding DMFB, existing resources, and resource needs.  Among 242 respondents across 42 states, perceived need for community-based depression services was high (8.7/10), and almost all reported they would consider implementing DMFB (94%). Most had some resources in place to support DMFB (e.g., technology, staff, experience with other evidence-based programs), but most indicated need for key program-specific resources, with the most critical resource needs being funding, dedicated personnel, and training (e.g., depression identification, DMFB delivery, and emergency management).

records.title: From Digital Engagement to in-Person Social Participation: Examining Associations Between Online Activities and Multiple Indicators of Social Participation Among Older Adults in Germany
records.abstract: Digital involvement shapes aging, with both positive and negative effects. This study examines how different Internet use types (social, information-seeking, entertainment) relate to older adults’ social participation, considering both  (social activity level) and perceived social participation (loneliness and sense of mattering i.e., feeling important to others). Furthermore, this study examined whether digital skills moderate the associations between Internet use and social participation outcomes. Cross-sectional data from 426 community-dwelling adults aged 50-95 (M = 69.1) in Germany were analyzed using hierarchical linear regressions and moderation analyses. Social use and information-seeking were positively associated with  social participation, while media streaming showed a negative association. More frequent social Internet use was associated with lower loneliness. Higher digital skill levels strengthened the negative association between social Internet use and loneliness. The findings suggest distinct associations between different types of Internet use and social participation, with digital skills potentially moderating these associations in later life.

records.title: Immediate task-specific and delayed generalized adaptations to variable dual-task training in community-dwelling older adults: a randomized waitlist-controlled trial
records.abstract: Aging is accompanied by progressive declines in cognitive and physical function. Dual-task training, which combines cognitive and motor demands, is a promising nonpharmacological approach, yet evidence that its benefits generalize beyond trained tasks and persist over time remains limited. This study examined the immediate and longer-term effects of a variable dual-task intervention on motor and cognitive function in community-dwelling older adults.  Fifty adults aged ≥ 65 years, including participants meeting criteria for mild cognitive impairment, were randomly allocated to an intervention group (IG; n = 30) or waitlist control (WLC; n = 20). The IG completed a 12-week, twice-weekly program (24 sessions × 60 min) designed to be highly variable across cognitive and motor demands to minimize task-specific learning. Outcomes were assessed at baseline, post-intervention, and three-month follow-up, including the Timed Up and Go Test, Five Times Sit-to-Stand Test (5xSTS), Eriksen Flanker Test, Trail Making Test, and Digit Span Test. Between-group effects and long-term trajectories within the IG were analyzed using linear and generalized linear mixed models under an intention-to-treat approach.  The intervention produced a significant improvement in functional lower-limb strength relative to the WLC at post-intervention (5xSTS: Group × Time interaction p = 0.005, standardized mean difference [SMD] = 0.54), maintained within the IG at three-month follow-up. No significant between-group effects were observed for the remaining motor or cognitive outcomes at post-intervention. Within the IG, improvements in functional mobility (Timed Up and Go, SMD = 0.28), inhibitory control (Flanker reaction time, SMD = 0.40–0.42), and short-term memory (forward Digit Span, SMD = 0.62) were absent immediately post-intervention and emerged only at follow-up.  Variable dual-task training produced immediate gains in functional lower-limb strength that persisted at follow-up, alongside delayed improvements in functional mobility, inhibitory control, and short-term memory consistent with a post-training consolidation process. These findings suggest two complementary pathways: task-specific overlap between training and assessment may explain the immediate motor gains, whereas variable practice may foster broader cognitive and mobility benefits that emerge over time. Trial registration German Clinical Trials Register, DRKS00038787 ( https://www.drks.de/DRKS00038787 ), retrospectively registered on 19/12/2025.

records.title: Multidimensional frailty trajectories and associated factors in older adults with pulmonary tuberculosis: a prospective longitudinal study
records.abstract: Older adults with pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) are particularly vulnerable to multidimensional frailty. However, longitudinal evidence regarding patterns of frailty changes after antituberculosis treatment initiation and their associated factors remains limited. This study aimed to identify distinct trajectories of multidimensional frailty among older adults with pulmonary TB and to examine the associations of anxiety, depression, insomnia, and clinical characteristics with different frailty trajectories.  A prospective longitudinal study was conducted among 251 older adults with pulmonary TB. Multidimensional frailty was assessed using the Tilburg Frailty Indicator (TFI) at 1, 3, 9, and 12 months after initiation of antituberculosis treatment. At baseline, anxiety and depression were assessed using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), and insomnia was assessed using the Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS). Latent class growth analysis was used to identify distinct trajectories of multidimensional frailty. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was subsequently applied to select candidate variables, followed by multinomial logistic regression to examine factors associated with trajectory membership.  Three distinct trajectories of multidimensional frailty were identified: high-frailty decreasing (13.1%), moderate-frailty improving (17.9%), and low-frailty persistent (68.9%) trajectory. Multinomial LASSO regression selected 14 candidate variables potentially associated with frailty trajectory membership. Compared with the low-frailty persistence trajectory, a history of smoking (OR = 4.668, 95% CI 1.217–7.904, P = 0.025) was associated with greater odds of membership in the high-frailty decreasing trajectory. In contrast, higher albumin levels (OR = 0.892, 95% CI 0.798–0.996, P = 0.043), absence of anxiety symptoms (OR = 0.093, P = 0.001), absence of depressive symptoms (OR = 0.044, P P  Multidimensional frailty exhibited substantial heterogeneity among older adults with pulmonary TB during antituberculosis treatment. Baseline anxiety, depressive symptoms, and insomnia, together with albumin level, were associated with distinct frailty trajectories. Early frailty screening during antituberculosis treatment, integrated with assessment of psychological and sleep status and routine laboratory indicators, may facilitate trajectory-based risk stratification and individualized management of frailty in older adults with pulmonary TB. records.title: Social Return on Investment (SROI) of the BrainTrack App for Monitoring Brain Health Among Older Australians
records.abstract: Timely diagnosis of dementia is critical, as early identification enables interventions that can meaningfully improve quality of life and support long-term planning for individuals and their families. Despite this, many Australians continue to receive a diagnosis at a late stage due to a range of personal, social, and structural barriers. BrainTrack, a freely available and evidence-based mobile application, was developed to help address this gap by supporting users to monitor their cognitive health and encouraging earlier engagement with healthcare professionals when concerns arise. This study sought to assess the broader social and economic value generated by BrainTrack. A Social Return on Investment (SROI) framework was employed to quantify the social outcomes associated with the app. Survey data collected 12 months after initial use captured five key outcomes: increased dementia literacy, enhanced dementia knowledge, reduced stigma, greater motivation to adopt cognitive health-promoting behaviours, and increased help-seeking intentions. Monetary values were assigned to each outcome to estimate the value created. Inputs included the resources invested in BrainTrack, such as initial development costs and ongoing maintenance. To determine the net impact, adjustments were made for deadweight, displacement, attribution, and drop-off prior to calculating the SROI ratio. Survey responses from 2,339 BrainTrack users informed the analysis. With an investment of AU$1.9 million over five years, the SROI analysis estimated a social return of approximately $5 for every $1 invested in BrainTrack. Sensitivity analyses showed ratios ranging from AU$0.86:1 to AU$24:1. The largest proportion of estimated social value was associated with increased motivation to change, whereas reduced stigma and increased help-seeking were associated with comparatively smaller estimated social value. Overall, BrainTrack was associated with social and economic value through cognitive self-monitoring, increased dementia awareness, and greater engagement with health services.

records.title: Timed Up and Go, gait speed, and grip strength: associations and discriminative performance for falls in community-dwelling older adults - results from the KORA-age study
records.abstract: Physical performance measures are commonly used in geriatric assessment and have been associated with falls, but their ability to discriminate between older adults with and without falls may be limited. We compared the Timed Up and Go (TUG) test, gait speed, and grip strength within a population-based cohort, considering associations, discriminatory performance, incremental discrimination, and established clinical TUG thresholds.  We analyzed data from 1,079 community-dwelling adults aged ≥ 65 years participating in KORA-Age. Fall status was classified for 819 participants based on self-reported falls in the 12 months preceding the 3-year follow-up interview. Associations of baseline TUG, gait speed, and grip strength with reported falls were examined using sequential logistic regression models adjusted for age and sex, additional clinical covariates, and frailty. Discriminatory performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with DeLong tests used to evaluate incremental discrimination beyond age and sex. We additionally examined combinations of the three performance measures and predefined TUG thresholds. Inverse-probability weighting was used in sensitivity analyses to address selective follow-up.  Poorer TUG performance remained associated with reported falls after additional adjustment for frailty (OR per 1-s increase 1.095, 95% CI 1.018–1.176), whereas the association with slower gait speed was attenuated after frailty adjustment and grip strength was not associated with falls. The age- and sex-adjusted reference model had an AUC of 0.680; corresponding AUCs after adding TUG, gait speed, or grip strength were 0.700, 0.692, and 0.675, respectively, with no clear evidence of incremental discrimination. Combining all three performance measures did not improve discrimination beyond TUG alone. Higher TUG thresholds identified smaller groups with a higher prevalence of falls and greater specificity but progressively lower sensitivity. Inverse-probability-weighted analyses yielded similar associations.  TUG remained associated with reported falls after multivariable and additional frailty adjustment, but none of the three physical performance measures showed clear incremental discrimination beyond age and sex. Combining the measures did not improve discrimination, and established TUG thresholds showed limited sensitivity. These findings support distinguishing statistical associations with falls from the ability of physical performance measures to discriminate between older adults with and without falls. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

records.title: Psychological costs of low wealth in midlife: Lower socioeconomic status carries greater disadvantage for depressive symptoms in the United States than Europe and China
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Socioeconomic inequalities in depressive symptoms are well documented, yet little is known about how these inequalities unfold during midlife and whether they vary across national and historical contexts.  Using harmonized longitudinal data spanning 1992 to 2022 from 16 countries (United States, England, France, Austria, Belgium, Germany, Switzerland, Israel, Italy, Spain, Greece, Denmark, Netherlands, Sweden, South Korea, and China), this study modeled trajectories of depressive symptoms among adults aged 45 to 65 across four wealth-based socioeconomic strata: Low (1st to 15th percentile), Lower-middle (16th to 45th), Upper-middle (46th to 75th), and High (76th to 100th).   revealed cross-national disparities: midlife adults in the United States reported higher depressive symptoms than their peers in most other nations, and this difference was most pronounced among lower SES groups. In most nations, later-born cohorts reported more depressive symptoms, with Upper-middle SES individuals exhibiting the largest historical increases. Beyond these mean-level patterns, lower SES groups were found to exhibit greater heterogeneity across three trajectory features of depressive symptoms (i.e., mean-levels at age 50 as well as linear and quadratic changes in depressive symptoms). This may suggest that under socioeconomic disadvantage, depressive symptoms are less tightly structured by SES alone and more strongly shaped by other contextual and individual factors. Discussion Collectively, findings highlight that mental health inequalities in midlife are deeply embedded in societal and historically changing structures. Policies that strengthen social protections and promote economic security may reduce these disparities and enhance well-being across the life course.

records.title: Operationalizing Cognitive Frailty: A Systematic Review of Definitions, Tools, and Measurement Inconsistencies
records.abstract: and  Cognitive frailty (CF), the co-occurrence of physical frailty and cognitive impairment without dementia, is a potentially reversible condition associated with adverse outcomes in older adults. However, heterogeneity in operational definitions and measurement approaches limits comparability and clinical translation. This review examined how CF has been defined and operationalized, including adaptations to established criteria. Research Design and  PubMed, Web of Science, and PsycINFO were searched for English-language studies published from 2013 through 2025. Eligible studies explicitly referred to CF in adults aged 50 years or older. Risk of bias was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute tools. Definitions, assessment tools, thresholds, and operational criteria were synthesized descriptively. Fried Phenotype (FP) implementation was examined using an adaptation-equivalence typology classifying domain-level measurement and threshold deviations.  Among 257 studies, 13 frailty and 26 cognitive assessment tools were identified. The FP was predominantly utilized (n = 164/257; 64%), although 68% (n = 112/164) modified the measurement method, threshold, or both in at least one domain. The Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) thresholds used to define cognitive impairment varied substantially, whereas all studies using the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) used a threshold of 0.5. Dementia was not explicitly excluded in 50 studies, despite its exclusion being a defining criterion of CF.  CF remains operationally heterogeneous. Updated international consensus and minimum reporting standards are needed to clarify core criteria and acceptable adaptations. FP-based studies should explicitly report domain-level modifications to improve comparability, reproducibility, and evidence synthesis.

records.title: Disruptions in Support Networks of People Living With Dementia: Evidence From a National Study of Caregiver Networks
records.abstract: People living with dementia rely on informal support that may be especially vulnerable to social restrictions such as those imposed during the COVID-19 pandemic.  To assess whether family and friends supporting adults with dementia were more likely to discontinue assistance during the pandemic than those supporting adults with other chronic conditions.  Using nationally representative data from 2,037 U.S. current caregivers reporting on 7,742 supporters within their care networks, multilevel logistic regression identified factors associated with discontinued support.  Ten percent of supporters withdrew help. Those assisting care recipients with dementia had higher odds of withdrawal (OR = 1.40, 95% CI 1.02–1.92). Supporters who were friends or distant relatives of the caregiver were more likely to withdraw than those who were close family, while strongly connected or dual-role supporters were less likely to withdraw (OR = 0.07, 95% CI 0.05–0.10). Higher caregiver income buffered against loss.

records.title: Parental Longevity and Cognitive Ability in Older Mexican Adults
records.abstract: Parental longevity is linked to better offspring cognition, with limited evidence from middle-income countries. We examined associations between parental longevity and cognition in Mexico while controlling for health, socioeconomic status (SES), and genetic factors.  We used the 2018 wave of the Mexican Health and Aging Study ( n = 5,049; age 65+). Maternal/paternal longevity was based on survival to age 85 or older. We used latent variable regressions to estimate associations with offspring cognition, adjusting for demographics, parental characteristics, health, health behaviors, SES, and APOE-ε4 carrier status.  About 31% of respondents had a mother and 31% had a father who survived to age 85 or older. Maternal, but not paternal, longevity was independently associated with better offspring cognition. The maternal association persisted after full adjustment.  Maternal longevity was positively linked to offspring cognition independent of health, health behaviors, SES, and APOE-ε4. Intergenerational support and broader genetic factors may contribute to this association.

records.title: Fertility and Later-Life Mental Health: Evidence on Transfers and Instrumental Assistance From Adult Children in Indonesia
records.abstract: This study examined whether completed fertility shapes later-life mental health in Indonesia and whether adult children’s support explains this relationship.  Using the 2007 and 2014 Indonesian Family Life Survey, we instrumented fertility with differential exposure to Village Contraceptive Distribution Centers and estimated 2SLS and instrumental-variables mediation models.  An additional child reduced CES-D score and probability of elevated depressive symptoms. Financial and material transfers formed a protective pathway, while the remaining component outside measured transfers offset part of this effect. Higher fertility also increased instrumental assistance, although its mediating contribution was imprecisely estimated. Protective effects were more apparent among respondents with less than primary education, alongside adverse physical and nutritional outcomes. Discussion Completed fertility may improve later-life mental health partly through transfers from adult children, while supportive and burdensome consequences coexist, especially among socioeconomically constrained older adults. Estimates apply to the fertility-responsive population identified by the IV design.

records.title: Finding the upsides to living alone: Adaptation and inequality among older U.S. adults?
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: This study investigates how the growing population of older Americans living alone adapts to daily life, testing three sociological hypotheses regarding “upsides” to solo living: spending more time outside, spending more time with non-residential ties, and spending more time in organized activities. We also consider whether such adaptations are unequal, investigating potential fault lines across key social categories including race/ethnicity, education, gender, and disability.  Using 2003–2019 American Time Use Survey data (N = 83,997), we employed multiple regression analysis to estimate both the likelihood of participation and the duration of time spent in each of these ways.   support the notion of locational and social adaptation: older adults living alone spend significantly more time outside the home and more time with friends and non-residential family than their co-resident peers. However, we found that solo dwellers spend less time in organized activities. Consistent with one dimension of the unequal adaptation hypothesis, several behavioral patterns were stratified by race/ethnicity, with Black older adults standing out from each of the other groups. Discussion Findings point to living alone as a distinct social ecology rather than a simple marker of deficit, with older adults adapting through the reorganization of daily exposure to people and places. This adaptation does not appear strongly structured by most social categories, though strong racialized differences suggest that future research should continue to assess the way diverse older Americans live together and with others.

records.title: Temporal Trends in the Prevalence of Frailty in England From 2002 to 2022, With Forecasts to 2040: Longitudinal Secondary Analysis of a National Cohort Study
records.abstract: The increasing life expectancy provides an opportunity for healthy longevity, but frailty is a potential challenge. Existing studies of frailty prevalence in England are largely cross-sectional, use heterogeneous frailty definitions, and rarely break down population-level drivers or project future burden, limiting their use for health and social care planning.  This study aimed to explore temporal trends of frailty prevalence and project scenario-based future prevalence up to 2040 for the community-dwelling population aged 50 years and older in England.  Prevalence of frailty (measured using a frailty index) in the overall sample and subgroups of age, sex, educational level, and marital status from 2002 to 2022 was estimated among the community-dwelling population aged 50 years and older using 10 waves of nationally representative data from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA; n=6226 to 11,218 across waves). The number of individuals with frailty was also derived in each year. Joinpoint regression models were used to explore temporal trends of frailty prevalence. A linear probability regression model was performed using pooled data from 10 waves of the ELSA to explore driving factors and project future prevalence. Decomposition analysis was used to estimate the contribution of individual factors to the change in prevalence.  A statistically nonsignificant ( P =.61) increase of 2.3 percentage points from 15.5% (1738/11,218) in 2002 to 17.8% (1108/6226) in 2022 was observed, with the number of individuals with frailty growing from 2,560,122 to 3,791,038 among community-dwelling adults aged 50 years and older in England. Those with advanced age, who were female, had a lower educational level, and/or were single had a consistently higher prevalence of frailty. Opposing contributions netted to this overall change: improvements in sociodemographic conditions and educational attainment and healthier lifestyle behaviors offset 222.5%, 94.9%, and 51.6% of the observed increase, respectively. Under scenario-based projections, prevalence was estimated at 20.5% (95% CI 19.2%-21.9%) in 2040, corresponding to 5,213,689 people with frailty.  Despite a modest increase in prevalence among the community-dwelling population aged 50 years and older, the substantial growth in the absolute number of individuals with frailty indicates a likely rise in future care demands. The study contributes a 20-year trend, decomposition, and forecast framework for community-dwelling older adults. Findings support prioritizing broader sociodemographic development alongside educational attainment and healthy lifestyles, with potential policy approaches including income and social protection, housing improvements, access to health care, and prevention. Key limitations include self-reported measures, exclusion of care home residents, and potential influence of unmeasured effects.

records.title: Unraveling the Early-Life Influences on Healthy Aging: Insights From the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS)
records.abstract: To examine the association between early-life circumstances and healthy aging among community-dwelling older Chinese adults.  Data were from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study. We used regression  to identify independent and joint associations of six early-life factors with healthy aging as assessed by the Chinese Healthy Aging Index (CHAI; 0–12), a composite score evaluating six physiological systems.  Of 3,069 participants, 4.82% had the healthiest CHAI score (0–2). After multivariable adjustment, personal education and family economic status were associated with healthier CHAI individually; the cumulative early-life score was associated with the CHAI, both dichotomously and continuously. Each additional score was associated with 37% (95% CI: 23%, 53%) higher odds of being in the healthiest CHAI category. Discussion Favorable early-life socioeconomic conditions support healthier aging among Chinese older adults, highlighting the need to address early-life inequalities to promote healthy aging.

records.title: Ambivalent close ties and cognitive functioning: Does coping play a role?
records.abstract: and  Close relationships that are characterized by both positive and negative qualities (i.e., ambivalent ties) are common in later life and often give rise to interpersonal tensions with deleterious consequences for well-being. However, little is known about their effect on cognitive health. These effects may depend on seldom-studied interpersonal coping strategies that may either stimulate or deplete cognitive resources. This study tested whether ambivalent ties relate to lower cognitive functioning among older adults, and whether interpersonal coping strategies moderate these associations. Research Design and  As part of the Daily Experiences and Well-being Study (DEWS), participants (N = 271, ages 65-89) completed an in-person baseline interview assessing positive and negative qualities of their close social relationships and overall cognitive functioning (composite of four tests), followed by a self-administered questionnaire assessing three interpersonal coping strategies (engaged, avoidant, destructive).  Linear regression models revealed that a greater proportion of ambivalent ties was associated with worse overall cognitive functioning, but this association was not moderated by any interpersonal coping strategy. Sensitivity analyses of the separate cognitive tests revealed, unexpectedly, that greater use of engaged coping strengthened the association between ambivalent ties and worse executive functioning performance.  A greater proportion of ambivalent ties in one’s social network is associated with lower cognitive functioning among older adults, a link that may not easily be buffered through coping.  suggest that ambivalent ties are an understudied important potential risk factor for adverse cognitive outcomes in later life.

records.title: The Experiences of Psychotherapy for People With Dementia: A Qualitative Interview Study With Family Members
records.abstract: Psychotherapeutic interventions can support people with dementia. Family members often play a pivotal role in the therapeutic process but little is known about their experiences of therapy, how they perceive the impact on their relative, and how the experience affects them directly. This study aimed to explore the experiences of family members who engage in therapy, or support someone living with dementia to attend therapy. Individuals with dementia and their family members were recruited as participants through NHS Trusts, professional networks, social media and community and support groups based in England and Wales. Semi-structured qualitative individual or dyadic interviews were conducted with 17 participants, eight of whom were living with dementia and nine were family members. Framework analysis was used. Family members highlighted “the importance of feeling seen” as distinct individuals by clinicians when engaging with psychotherapy, and not just the carer of their partner. When working with “dementia as dynamic phenomenon”, therapeutic approaches needed to balance being sufficiently structured and containing whilst allowing for adaptions to each individual changeable presentation. Participants highlighted how psychotherapy presented “expected and unexpected outcomes”, challenges that arose when outcomes were not agreed upon, and how therapy functioned as a support structure in ways the participants did not foresee. Psychotherapeutic intervention provides meaningful support to the family members of individuals with dementia. Understanding the needs of family members, alongside the needs of the individual with dementia, and taking a systemic approach is conducive to better therapeutic outcomes. The changeable nature of dementia presentation means that a therapeutic approach should be flexible based on the needs of the family. Psychotherapeutic intervention with individuals with dementia can have a range of benefits for the individual and the wider family, when sufficient considerations are made to understand each person’s needs.

records.title: Economic evaluation of the annual and daily costs of the adult foster care model for older dependent adults: Insights from the Karukera Study of Aging in Foster Families
records.abstract: and  Adult foster care may represent a viable alternative to nursing homes for dependent older adults. This study aimed to estimate the annual and daily cost of adult foster care for older adults. Research Design and  The Karukera Study of Aging in Foster Families is a prospective, one-year observational study including adults aged 60+ living in adult foster care in the French Caribbean Islands. We measured healthcare resource utilization using the RUD (Resource Utilization in Dementia)-Lite instrument. Costs related to healthcare consumption, foster caregiver remuneration, and training were estimated and expressed per patient-year.  A total of 106 older adults (mean age: 82.2±11.2 years; 61.3% women) were followed for one year (mean follow-up duration: 306.1±90.8 days). The daily cost of outpatient care was estimated at €33.3, of which €29.9 corresponded to community nursing visits. Caregiver remuneration and training represented a daily expenditure of €62.8 per older adult. The total annual cost of adult foster care was estimated at €35,076, or €96.1 per resident per day. Hospitalization costs were estimated at €224.0 per patient-year, while emergency department visits accounted for €42.0 per patient-year.  Compared with a daily cost of €121 per resident in metropolitan nursing homes and €150 per resident in nursing homes in the French Caribbean Islands, adult foster care reduced costs by 20.6% and 35.9%, respectively. In the context of constrained healthcare budgets and increasing demand for long-term care related to dependency, adult foster care may represent a scalable and economically sustainable alternative. records.abstract: : Family co-residence is often considered protective for older adults in India but may not ensure inclusion in household decisions. There was little evidence that widowhood and exclusion interacted. Associations with depressive symptoms were more clearly observed among women than men. : Among co-resident older adults, having a meaningful voice in family decisions may be important for mental health beyond shared residence alone.

records.title: Mastery as a Mediator for the Effects of Work Discrimination on Racial Disparities in Life Satisfaction
records.abstract: We examine racial disparities in the association between work discrimination and life satisfaction among older adults and whether any differences are mediated by one’s sense of personal mastery using data from the 2010 and 2012 waves of the Health and Retirement Study. The  from the structural equation models (SEM) show White people who experience work discrimination report the lowest life satisfaction, followed by Hispanic and then Black people. After accounting for the mediating effect of one’s sense of mastery to cope with discriminatory work experiences, we find work discrimination still has a direct negative association with the life satisfaction of White and Black respondents but the effect for Hispanic people is no longer statistically significant. The  of the direct and total effects also suggest the mediating effects of mastery on the association between work discrimination and life satisfaction among older workers is strongest for White people, followed by Hispanic people and then Black people. These findings suggest that a person’s efficiency at drawing upon their coping resources like mastery when needed is essential for protecting their well-being from the harmful effects of work discrimination, especially for Black and Hispanic people.

records.title: Double Scaffold of Retirement on Subsequent Health: Revisiting Spatio-Temporality and Finance Through the Feature-Wide Effect Heterogeneity
records.abstract: This study investigates how retirement’s effect on subsequent health varies by individual attributes and their interaction. Instead of spotlighting heterogeneity for a specific, theoretically predetermined feature, I consider the feature-wide effect heterogeneity to find possible data-driven candidates that generate this heterogeneity. To accomplish this, I use causal forests and harmonized data from the Gateway to Global Aging Data (the Gateway). The  show that temporal dimensions (such as age and birth cohort) and financial dimensions (such as income and wealth) are the most important features in heterogenizing retirement’s effect on health. Based on these findings, I suggest the “double scaffold” model to comprehensively explain feature-wide effect heterogeneity.

records.title: The experience of family caregivers when their loved one is home hospitalized: a mixed methods analysis of a randomized controlled trial
records.abstract: Home hospital has been shown to achieve comparable, if not better, clinical and patient-centred outcomes compared to brick-and-mortar (BAM) hospitalisation. Family caregivers (FCs) play an essential role in delivering home hospital care; however, their perceptions towards the home hospital model remain an active area of inquiry, particularly in rural settings.  We conducted a mixed  analysis of FCs of patients participating in a multicenter randomised controlled trial of rural home hospital in the USA and Canada. We compared pre- and post-intervention burden among home hospital and BAM caregivers with the Zarit Burden Interview-12 (ZBI-12) scale (n = 20 home hospital, n = 10 BAM). We conducted semi-structured qualitative interviews with home hospital caregivers (n = 19). Qualitative data were coded and analysed using thematic analysis to construct core themes and subthemes.  There was no significant difference in median ZBI-12 scores between home hospital and BAM at admission (4 interquartile range [IQR 2–9.3] vs 5 [IQR 0.3–9.3]; P = .723), discharge (6 [3.3–8] vs 7.5 [2.5–11.8], P = .309), or change from admission to discharge (0 [−2.5 to 3] vs 1.5 [0–3.5]; P = .269). Our qualitative analysis revealed three central themes: (i) The caregiving experience was positively shaped by strong communication and shared decision-making with the care team; (ii) Caregivers described receiving high-quality home hospital care, particularly surrounding patient-centeredness and technology; and (iii) Home hospital was perceived to offer greater flexibility, comfort and psychosocial support compared to BAM hospitalisation.  Home hospital provides numerous benefits for FCs without increasing perceived burden; further work is needed to establish potential supports to optimise their experience.

records.title: Effects of esketamine on postoperative sleep quality in elderly patients under general anesthesia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
records.abstract: Postoperative sleep disturbance (PSD) is a common disorder among elderly patients undergoing surgery and is associated with a higher risk of adverse outcomes. This meta-analysis investigated the effects of esketamine on postoperative sleep quality among elderly patients.  PubMed, Embase, The Cochrane Library, CNKI, and Wanfang databases were searched to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing intravenous esketamine with control in elderly patients (≥ 60 years) undergoing elective surgery in general anesthesia. Sleep quality on postoperative day (POD) 1 was the primary outcome. Other outcomes included sleep quality at other time points,  sleep parameters, pain, cognitive function, and adverse events.  Seventeen RCTs involving 2587 patients were included. Regarding the primary outcome, esketamine significantly improved subjective sleep quality on POD 1 (SMD = -0.72; 95% CI, -1.10 to -0.34; I² = 93%), POD 2 (SMD = -1.40; 95% CI, -2.15 to -0.64; I² = 97%), and POD 7 (SMD = -0.38; 95% CI, -0.62 to -0.14; I² = 53%).  sleep measures on POD 1 revealed longer total sleep time, reduced sleep latency, and improved sleep efficiency. Esketamine also decreased pain intensity (SMD = -0.63; 95% CI, -0.88 to -0.38; I² = 70%) and improved MMSE scores (SMD = 0.65; 95% CI, 0.42 to 0.89; I² = 0%). Esketamine was associated with a lower risk of nausea or vomiting. No significant differences was observed between the two groups in terms of dizziness, while hypotension occurred less frequently with esketamine.  Among elderly surgical patients, perioperative esketamine was associated with improved postoperative sleep quality, reduced pain intensity, and a potential improvement in cognitive function, without a significant increase in the risk of major adverse events. However, high-quality RCTs are needed to confirm these findings and determine optimal dosing regimens. Of note, all 17 included trials were conducted in China, potentially limiting the generalizability of our findings to other populations.

records.title: Eight-week omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation alters but does not attenuate exercise-induced muscle damage in older adults: a randomised controlled trial
records.abstract: Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) serves as a model to study muscle plasticity and recovery. Exercise recovery declines with age, and while omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (n-3 PUFA) exhibit inconsistent effects in younger adults, the effect in older adults is unknown.  In a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial, 43 healthy, older women and men (65-85 years) ingested 5 mL of n-3 PUFA algae oil (2 g PUFA) or placebo for eight weeks. After eight weeks participants performed a bout of 10 × 10 eccentric-emphasised leg extensions. Outcome measures included quadriceps maximal voluntary contraction (MVC), muscle soreness, creatine kinase (CK) and inflammation (Interleukin-6, high-sensitive C-reactive protein; CRP) assessed at baseline and post-exercise.  EIMD symptoms such as muscle soreness and function were modest and consistent with previous reports in older adults. Overall, n-3 PUFA supplementation did not improve functional recovery. However, a borderline greater MVC loss was observed in the n-3 PUFA group (time × group: P = .064), which resulted from significantly lower MVC in the n-3 PUFA group at 24 h (difference: −10.9%, 95%CI: −21.4;−0.40%, P = .042) and at 72 h (difference: −9.80, 95%CI: −18.3;−1.27, P = .025) post-exercise compared to the placebo. No significant overall group differences were observed for CK, interleukin-6, CRP, but CK concentrations significantly increased from baseline at 24 h post-exercise in the placebo group (change: +81.1%, 95%CI:10.5;152%, P = .014). Habitual physical activity and sex emerged as significant moderators of molecular recovery in an exploratory analysis.  n-3 PUFA supplementation did not improve functional recovery, but different molecular response patterns were observed. Habitual physical activity and sex may be determinants of post-exercise response; this exploratory finding warrants confirmation in larger studies.

records.abstract: More than 60% of older workers report experiencing ageism in the workplace, yet little is known about whether the relationship between ageism, job satisfaction, and mental health differs by US-born status. This study examined whether job satisfaction mediates the association between workplace ageism and depressive symptoms and assessed whether this association differs by US-born status. Data were drawn from the 2018 and 2020 National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1979 for workers aged 53- 62, and a multiple-group path analysis was conducted. The  indicated that, among US-born workers, job satisfaction significantly mediated the associations between depressive symptoms and both ageism in promotion and ageism in early retirement. Among immigrant workers, however, this mediating effect was significant only for ageism in promotion. Findings underscore the importance of developing anti-ageism policies that adopt an intersectional approach, jointly considering US-born status and age to reduce the detrimental impacts of ageism on workers’ mental health.

records.title: Changes in Instrumental Support Around Retirement: Longitudinal Evidence From Europe
records.abstract: As populations age and the share of retirees increases across Europe, the question of whether individuals stay active after retirement is increasingly salient. Retirees are known to provide more instrumental support than their working counterparts. However, most previous studies have relied on between-group comparisons of retirees and employed individuals, leaving it unclear how the transition into retirement affects changes in instrumental support within individuals over time. Using eight waves of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe covering 19 countries between 2004–2022 (n = 7,422 observations from 3,711 individuals aged 50+), we employed fixed-effects regression and found that the transition from employment to retirement was associated with an increase in instrumental support provision outside the household. We also found suggestive evidence that this association was stronger in countries with higher social expenditures. These findings indicate that retirement may promote activity and facilitate engagement in helping others.

records.abstract: Cognitive training may enhance cognition and support brain health during aging, but few trials have evaluated readily accessible chatbot-based programs with neuroimaging outcomes. records.title: Living Alone With Dementia: Managing Without Informal Support to Contact and Navigate Services
records.abstract: Purpose: People with dementia can and do live successfully on their own, but there are additional challenges for people living alone without informal support. This paper reports findings of the first study in the UK to examine needs and experiences of, and services for, people with dementia who live alone without informal support. Method: The study involved a service audit of 13 local authority commissioners in two English regions, interviews with 22 people with dementia who live alone without informal carers, and case studies of four services supporting this group. Findings: Awareness of this population among commissioners was limited. There were very few services which explicitly supported this group, and some mainstream services excluded people without carers. None of the local authorities collected data on numbers of people with dementia living alone, or those without informal support, in their area. Some participants with dementia had contacted social care, but this had not always resulted in appropriate support, and people reported problematic interactions with staff, assumptions that friends would provide care, and support not being available at the right time. Self-funders were left with little support. People with dementia were resourceful, using general services, technology, and other tactics, including cleaners, meal delivery, community taxis, and automatic reminders to organise their lives. However, as many of these additional services have a cost attached, there is potential to exacerbate existing inequalities. Participants wanted more support, particularly with finances and administrative tasks. Services can help this group with supported handovers, allowing self-referral back into a service, and keeping case files open. : Both the number of people with dementia, and the number of people ageing without children, are rising, and it will therefore become increasingly important to facilitate effective support for people with dementia to live independently without informal support.

records.title: Comparative Effectiveness of Digital Exercise-Based Interventions for Improving Balance in Older Adults: Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis With GRADE Certainty of Evidence
records.abstract: Technology-based rehabilitation is increasingly used for balance training in older adults. A 2023 network meta-analysis (NMA) found only exergaming with motion capture superior to no treatment; however, the evidence has since expanded, and no GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) appraisal has been applied.  This study aimed to update the comparative effectiveness of 5 technology categories—exergaming with balance platforms (EBP), exergaming with motion capture (EMC), other serious games, interventions with wearables, and telerehabilitation (Tele)—versus conventional exercise (CE), and no treatment (NT), applying GRADE adapted for NMA.  A systematic search of 4 databases from inception through April 2025, with an identical supplementary update search to January 31, 2026, identified 60 randomized controlled trials (N=3469; mean age 73.1, SD 5.2; range 63.3-86.2 y). Fifty-seven trials (2758 analyzed participants) contributed to 4 prespecified networks (all balance, functional scales, Timed Up and Go [TUG] test, and gait speed). A random-effects NMA was fitted using multivariate meta-regression. Treatment hierarchies were summarized by the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) and the probability of being best; certainty of evidence was rated with GRADE adapted for NMA.  In the all-balance network, Tele (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.69, 95% CI 0.08‐1.29; P =.03), EBP (SMD 0.63, 95% CI 0.31‐0.95; P P =.002), and CE (SMD 0.35, 95% CI 0.03‐0.68; P =.03) were superior to NT, with consistent findings in the TUG network (EBP 0.81, 95% CI 0.42‐1.20; Tele 0.82, 95% CI 0.16‐1.49; EMC 0.79, 95% CI 0.36‐1.21; all P P =.41).  Tele, EBP, and EMC were each associated with improved balance versus NT, although none exceeded CE. The first-place SUCRA ranking of Tele is preliminary. Certainty was moderate only for EBP and EMC versus NT on the TUG test; the remaining evidence is too uncertain for firm clinical recommendations. As no included trial reported falls, these findings are not direct evidence of fall prevention. Larger trials with standardized comparator intensity and posttraining follow-up are required.

records.title: Detection of Age-Related Cognitive Decline Over Short Time Frames Using Digital Multiday Learning Assessments: Longitudinal Study
records.abstract: High-resolution digital cognitive tools administered at frequent intervals enable the study of age-related cognitive change at a previously unattainable level of granularity. Computational modeling further enables the simultaneous examination of multiple aspects of cognitive performance.  The  of this study was to examine whether repeated digital multiday learning assessments can detect age-related cognitive decline over short time frames in cognitively unimpaired older adults and to quantify age-related differences in process-based cognitive markers derived from computational modeling.  A total of 209 cognitively unimpaired older adults (mean age 73.6, SD 8.2 years; n=136, 65.1% female) from the Harvard Aging Brain Study and affiliated studies were administered the Boston Remote Assessment for Neurocognitive Health, which includes the face-name task, a paired associative learning task. Daily median response times for correct responses were used as the primary outcome. A new version of the face-name task was administered across up to 4 testing intervals over a mean of 2.8 (SD 0.4) years. Using computational modeling, we estimated longitudinal changes in peak performance, a practice-adjusted marker of an individual’s best expected response time, as an indicator of age-related cognitive decline. We further examined age-related differences in peak performance, stability (within-person variability), learning within and across testing intervals, and between-interval forgetting, with embedded linear regressions for age, sex, years of education, and device type. records.title: A Longitudinal Study on Social Isolation, Chronic Diseases, and Depressive Symptoms: Evidence From the Korean Longitudinal Study of Aging
records.abstract: This study examined the longitudinal effects of social isolation on chronic diseases and depressive symptoms among middle-aged and older adults in South Korea, with attention to gender and age differences. Method Using data from three waves of the Korean Longitudinal Study of Aging, longitudinal path analysis was conducted on 5,585 participants.  Women and older adults showed higher levels of social isolation, chronic diseases, and depressive symptoms, indicating greater vulnerability. Significant longitudinal and bidirectional associations emerged among social isolation, chronic diseases, and depressive symptoms over time. While gender differences in long-term patterns were modest, age-related disparities were more substantial.  These findings underscore the importance of strengthening community-based social networks and implementing both conventional outreach—such as home visits—and innovative approaches, including technology-assisted companionship, to identify socially isolated individuals, particularly older adults.

records.title: Need-Conditioned Uncertainty and Perceived Non-Provision of Community Services: Social Participation and Functional Status Among Older Adults in Urban China
records.abstract: Older adults who need community services may remain uncertain whether those services are locally provided or judge that they are not. Research on perceived unmet need often combines these positions. Using a cross-sectional survey of 929 adults aged 60 or older in urban Jiangsu, China, we paired reported need with perceived provision across 20 services and distinguished awareness gaps, perceived non-provision, and comparison uncertainty for services not reported as needed. Fractional logit models examined associations with social participation and functional status. Greater social participation was associated with fewer awareness gaps, concentrated among adults with ADL disability (−8.75 percentage points per SD). A weaker, less stable association with perceived non-provision appeared among functionally independent adults, and no counterpart appeared for comparison uncertainty. Unresolved uncertainty and negative provision judgments may call for different responses, and outreach may be especially relevant for older adults with ADL disability.

records.title: Third Places, Walkable Access, and Neighborhood Satisfaction Among Older Adults
records.abstract: Neighborhood satisfaction is a key indicator of well-being and community quality of life, yet its relationship with third place engagement remains underexplored.  This study examines how third place engagement, access, and perceived built environments relate to physical livability, social connectedness, and overall neighborhood satisfaction among older adults.  Survey data were collected from 515 adults aged 65 and older in the Orlando area, and separate Ordinary Least Squares regression models were used.  The  indicate that neighborhood satisfaction is multidimensional, with shared yet distinct correlates across domains. Third place engagement and walkable access were consistently associated with all three outcomes. Socially oriented third place use was more closely tied to social connectedness, while built environment quality aligned with physical livability. Overall satisfaction reflected both domains, highlighting the value of viewing neighborhood satisfaction as related but distinct constructs shaped by functional and social experiences among older adults.

records.title: Delirium Occurrence and Associated Factors Among Patients With Dementia and Mild Cognitive Impairment Admitted to Long-Term Care Hospitals: Cross-Sectional Study
records.abstract: Delirium is common among older adults, particularly those with cognitive impairment. However, delirium among patients with dementia or mild cognitive impairment (MCI) in long-term care (LTC) hospitals has received limited attention.  This study aimed to examine delirium occurrence and associated factors among patients with dementia or MCI in LTC hospitals.  This cross-sectional study included 142 patients aged 65 years or older with dementia (n=100, 70.4%) or MCI (n=42, 29.6%) at 2 LTC hospitals in South Korea between September 2021 and August 2022. Delirium occurrence was defined as at least 1 positive Short Confusion Assessment Method assessment during twice-daily assessments over 4 weeks, including the first assessment. Multivariable logistic regression examined associated factors overall and within each cognitive group.  Delirium was identified in 55 (38.7%) of 142 patients. The proportion was 41% (41/100) in patients with dementia and 33.3% (14/42) in patients with MCI. Hypoactive delirium was the most common subtype (33/55, 60%). Overall, female sex (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 4.344, 95% CI 1.794-10.515; P=.001), immobility (aOR 4.953, 95% CI 1.857-13.205; P=.001), and analgesic use (aOR 3.641, 95% CI 1.262-10.501; P=.02) were associated with delirium. Infection was inversely associated with delirium (aOR 0.251, 95% CI 0.101-0.623; P=.003). In patients with dementia, female sex, immobility, analgesic use, and pain were associated with delirium. Diaper use was associated with delirium in patients with MCI.  Delirium was common among patients with dementia or MCI in LTC hospitals. The findings support regular delirium assessment, with attention to mobility and pain-related care needs. Further studies are needed to clarify the factors associated with delirium in each cognitive group.
